_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Science unit lecture film, Lesson 6 Food Chains. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON['lecture'] in order (producers; consumers; the arrow; breaking a link; chains and people), with the lesson's sorting step placed after the consumers, in the lesson's own words: its food chain sim (ART.kit.foodChainSvg, grass, rabbit and fox built link by link and then broken), its eight sorting animals and their two bins, its card-and-string physical model, and its four things people do.
title: Food Chains
subtitle: Grade 3 Science
objectives: Identify and describe simple food chains, where plants are producers and animals are consumers of plants and/or other animals.
Know that life processes common to plants and animals include nutrition, growth, movement and reproduction.
Use observations and tests to sort, group and classify objects.
Draw a diagram to represent a real world situation and/or scientific idea.
Talk about how science helps us understand our effect on the world around us.

beats.say: Every animal has to eat. But where does its food really come from?
Follow the food back, and every chain starts at the same place: a plant.
A plant does not eat. It makes its own food from sunlight, water and air.
Because it produces food, we call it a producer.
Grass is a producer. It does not eat anything at all.
Every food chain starts with a plant, and the plant's food starts with the Sun.
An animal cannot make food. It has to eat.
A rabbit eats the grass. An animal that eats is a consumer.
A fox eats the rabbit. The fox is a consumer too.
Grass, rabbit, fox. A food chain shows who eats whom.
Plants are producers. Animals are consumers. That is the whole rule.
An oak tree, seagrass and a dandelion all make their own food.
An owl, a fish and a rabbit cannot. They have to eat, so they are consumers.
A cow makes milk, but it eats grass. Eating makes it a consumer.
We draw a food chain with arrows. Grass, arrow, rabbit, arrow, fox.
The arrow means is eaten by. Grass is eaten by the rabbit.
It points from the food to the animal that eats it.
So the arrow goes from the grass to the rabbit, never the other way.
A drawing like this is a diagram: a model of who eats whom.

at.model: a model of who eats whom

beats.say: Now make a chain you can hold. Draw grass, a rabbit and a fox on three cards.

at.make: make a chain you can hold

beats.say: Tie the rabbit card under the grass card, and the fox under the rabbit.
Hold up the grass card. The whole chain hangs from it. That is a physical model.
Now let go of the grass card, and watch. The whole chain falls.

at.letgo: let go of the grass card

beats.say: No grass, no rabbit. No rabbit, no fox. Every link needs the one before it.
Spray the weeds and the plants die. No plants, no caterpillars.
No caterpillars, and the birds that eat them go hungry. Three links gone, from one spray.
Oil in the pond blocks the light. The pondweed dies, then the snails, the frogs, the heron.
Plant a hedge and you plant a producer. Insects come, then birds, and a new chain starts.
Science shows us what our actions do to the living things around us.
A plant is the producer. It makes its own food from sunlight.
Every animal is a consumer, because it has to eat.
The arrow means is eaten by. Draw the chain, or hold it on cards.
Take the plant away and the whole chain falls. That is why what we do matters.
